newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin recalls shame of anti-Jewish looting night.
newsitem.headline: Berlin recalls shame of anti-Jewish looting night.

text.p: Berlin Mayor Eberhard Diepgen said on Sunday the German nation had utterly failed in its duty to protect its own citizens 58 years ago when Nazis ransacked Jewish shops and synagogues on "Kristallnacht."
Speaking at a ceremony marking the anniversary of Kristallnacht, Diepgen said the state was no longer civilised when it allowed Germans to attack Germans.
The leader of Berlin's vestigial Jewish community, Jerzy Kanal, said Germans needed to remain on the watch for anti-democratic forces in the country.
He said that even though the number of attacks by neo-Nazis had declined recently, far-right groups were still active.

"In the night of November 9 to November 10 (1938), barbarism broke out here in the middle of Europe," Kanal said. "And the whole world watched in silence. The Nazis were given a green light to on this night for their later crimes."
Kanal said it was lamentable that 58 years ago there wasn't even a hint of protest by the Germans themselves.
The Nazis looted more than 7,000 Jewish shops and burned hundreds of synagogues across Germany on November 9, 1938.
"The 9th of November and what followed will remain in our hearts and minds as a warning," Diepgen said in his address at the Jewish community centre. "Intolerance can never again be accepted."
The Kristallnacht attacks were remembered at numerous ceremonies in Berlin, a city where the Jewish culture thrived before the Nazis took power.

Berlin was one of the world's 10 largest Jewish centres and many of Germany's leading scientists were Berlin Jews. There were about 160,000 Jews in Berlin in 1933, but only 1,400 were still in the city in 1945.
The rest emigrated or were killed in Nazi death camps. The size of the Jewish community in Berlin is now about 10,000.

Several hundred left-wing demonstrators, accompanied by hundreds of police officers, marched in the Moabit district of west Berlin carrying signs reading "Don't let anyone forget" and "Prevent pogroms, kill racism".
